Sources: abu-dhabi/AUTHORITY-MAP-ABU-DHABI.md + SPEED-RULES-ABU-DHABI.md + TOURISM-DEMAND-ABU-DHABI.md + REVENUE-STACK-ABU-DHABI.md + CREW-COST-ABU-DHABI.md + GEOMETRY-ABU-DHABI.json. CONTRACT v3: only `title` (<=6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (<=140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Underscore-prefixed fields (_contract, _internal, _guard and similar) NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Posture per the international addendum: the emirate already operates public marine transport, so the page leads with the authority's own operating record and the ask is 'extend your marine network'. Emirate-internal corridors only — inter-emirate service is a later-phase roadmap item and is not rendered anywhere in this file. Disclosure rail: the waterways custodian is referred to always and only as 'Abu Dhabi Maritime' — no parent-group naming anywhere. No counterparty identities, no program or fleet commitments, no launch dates, no ridership claims (none primary-sourced).

fn1.text: The Regulatory Bylaw for Maritime Safety in the Waterways of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi was announced by the Department of Municipalities and Transport on 11 July 2025, referenced as Administrative Decision No. (69) of 2025 — licensing, operational conduct, environmental obligations and emergency duties, with Abu Dhabi Maritime and the Integrated Transport Centre as implementing bodies.

fn2.text: Operating record as published by Abu Dhabi Maritime: two new fast ferries inaugurated in May 2025 serving Dalma Island — 193 passengers and 25 vehicles each at 35 knots, two daily round trips — with Saadiyat Marina & Ferry Terminal and Rabdan Marina opened 2024 and Al Aliah Island Ferry Terminal opened February 2025.

fn3.text: Scheduled public water transport per the official UAE government listing: daily water-taxi routes linking Yas Bay with Al Raha Beach (Al Zeina, Al Muneera, Al Bandar), Yas Marina and Al Qana Marina, and a Saadiyat–Al Aliah ferry.

fn4.text: Visitor-economy figures from the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi: 26.6 million visitors to the emirate in 2025, 5.9 million hotel guests (+2.2%) at 81% occupancy, 8.6 million cultural-site visits including 1.4 million at Louvre Abu Dhabi, and 2.2 million business-event delegates.

fn5.text: Abu Dhabi Maritime publishes its waterway speed limits on official safety maps: 5 knots within 50 metres of shore and marine facilities, 8 knots under bridge arches, 20 knots in channels, 50 knots on open water, and 20 knots on all waters after sunset. Every time on this page is planned at those posted limits; evening times use the night cap.

fn6.text: The Zaya Nurai island resort is reported temporarily closed for renovation in 2026; its jetty renders with that status stated and no demand modeled. Lulu Island has no verified public facility and renders as an experience anchor only.

fn7.text: The Mangrove National Park is managed by the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi. Wake, noise and wildlife protection are the stated purposes of the no-wake and protected-water rules; a purpose-based allowance would be a licensing conversation with the regulator — no allowance is assumed anywhere on this page.

fn8.text: Field trials of an autonomous vessel at Saadiyat, run under the emirate's Smart and Autonomous Systems Council with the Integrated Transport Centre, as published by the Abu Dhabi Media Office.

fn9.text: Road congestion per the TomTom Traffic Index 2025: Abu Dhabi average congestion 29.6%, 57 hours a year lost in rush hour, and a 10 km drive averaging 21 minutes 40 seconds citywide.

gap.title: Abu Dhabi already runs the network

copy.lead: This city is not waiting to be convinced about water transport. Abu Dhabi runs scheduled public ferries and water taxis across its islands today, opened three purpose-built marine facilities in 2024–25, and codified a single maritime safety framework for its waterways in 2025.
copy.support: The direction is written down: an integrated transport authority across land and marine modes, a single waterways custodian with published speed rules, a safety framework with special emphasis on marine environmental protection, and autonomous marine trials already on the water at Saadiyat. A zero-emission foiling tier is additive capacity on the network the emirate already runs.

plans.note: Two 35-knot fast ferries entered service in May 2025 — 193 passengers and 25 vehicles each. The emirate already commissions fast vessels.
Daily scheduled water taxis link Yas Bay, Yas Marina, Al Raha Beach and Al Qana, with a Saadiyat–Al Aliah ferry alongside.
Saadiyat Marina & Ferry Terminal and Rabdan Marina opened 2024; Al Aliah Island Ferry Terminal followed in February 2025.

plans.quote: Through this integrated regulatory framework, we aim to improve the efficiency of maritime operations, safeguard the environment, promote the safe and sustainable use of our waterways… to support our vision for a safer and more sustainable future.
plans.note: One framework for licensing, conduct and environmental protection — implemented by the waterways custodian with the transport authority.
Autonomous-vessel field trials are already running at Saadiyat — new marine technology is an active program, not a concept.

copy.framing: One conversation, not two. Abu Dhabi already operates public water transport across its islands under a single integrated transport authority — the posture here is extension: a fast, zero-emission tier on the marine network the emirate already runs and keeps growing.
copy.enable_track: License the vessels and grant landing access at existing marine terminals, marinas and water-taxi stops. Private capital finances the fleet; the ask is licensing and access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Procure or concession the foiling tier the way marine transit is procured today — new fast lines above the ferry and water-taxi fleet, integrated with the authority's network, with fares set with the authority.

operate_proof_points.proof: The emirate's integrated transport authority plans, regulates and operates public transport across land and marine modes — and keeps commissioning new marine services and facilities.

Single custodian of the emirate's waterways — vessel licensing, published safety maps and speed limits, public marinas and harbours with published berth tariffs, and day-to-day ferry and water-taxi operations.
Two 35-knot fast ferries inaugurated in May 2025 and three new marine facilities opened since 2024 — extension is already the operating rhythm, and a foiling tier continues it.

copy.headline: Abu Dhabi publishes its speed limits. We plan to them.
copy.framing: The emirate's safety maps codify the waterway rules: 5 knots near shore and marine facilities, 8 knots under bridges, 20 knots in channels, 50 knots on open water, and 20 knots everywhere after sunset. Every time on this page is planned at those posted limits — including evening runs timed at the night cap.
copy.ask: In protected and no-wake waters, the rules exist to control wake, noise and disturbance to wildlife. A foiling, electric vessel serves those purposes by design — where independent measurement confirms it, purpose-based relief is a conversation with the regulator, shown here only as what it would unlock.

expander.title: What purpose-based relief unlocks
body: The published rules separate the number from the purpose: no-wake zones protect shorelines, moorings and marine facilities, and the 2025 maritime framework places special emphasis on marine environmental protection — including the mangrove waters managed as a national park. A foiling vessel at speed produces near-zero wake and runs near-silent on electric power, serving those stated purposes better than displacement hulls at the same speed.

No relief is assumed anywhere on this page: every base time uses the posted limits, and evening times use the after-dark cap. Purpose-based relief in mangrove and no-wake waters would compress inner-corridor legs — rendered only as this labeled sensitivity, never in base times.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: Abu Dhabi's water-transport landscape is compact and clearly mandated. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: The emirate's integrated transport authority — plans, regulates and operates public transport across land and marine modes, commissions ferries and marine facilities, and co-implements the 2025 maritime safety framework. The primary counterpart for a foiling tier.

Emirate-level municipal and transport policy — issued the 2025 Regulatory Bylaw for Maritime Safety and attests marina berth-lease contracts. The policy umbrella above the transport and maritime bodies.

Single custodian of Abu Dhabi's waterways — licenses vessels and crews, publishes the safety maps and speed limits, manages public marinas and harbours with published berth tariffs, and operates the ferry and water-taxi services.

bodies.body: Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi (DCT)
bodies.role: Destination strategy and tourism data — steward of a visitor economy of 26.6 million visitors and 5.9 million hotel guests in 2025, the demand side of the tourism-weighted corridors on this network.

Manages marine protected areas including the Mangrove National Park — protected-water access conditions and wildlife rules. A zero-wake, zero-emission fleet is the natural permitting fit for protected waters.
